slides.say: For which of the following operations is a star b equal to b star a, for all numbers a and b?

So they ask when the order of the two inputs doesn't matter, for every a and b. [short pause] We'll solve it two ways, plugging in numbers to knock out choices, and then algebra to prove the one that's left.
at: the order of the two inputs

slides.say: [short pause] To show that a rule doesn't always work, one example where it fails is enough. Let's take a is one and b is two. Why not two equal numbers? Because with equal numbers, swapping them changes nothing, in every rule. So they can't knock anything out.
Choice number one, a squared times b. One star two is one squared times two, which is two. Two star one is two squared times one, which is four. Two is not four, so choice number one is out.
at: One star two is one squared
so choice number one is out

slides.say: Choice number two, a times, in brackets, a plus b. One star two is one times three, which is three. Two star one is two times three, which is six. Out. Choice number four, the bracket a minus b, squared, plus a. One star two: one minus two is negative one, and negative one squared is one. Then we add a, which is one, so one plus one is two. Two star one: two minus one is one, and one squared is one. Now a is two, so one plus two is three. Out.
at: so one plus two is three

slides.say: Choice number three, a b plus a plus b. One star two is two plus one plus two, which is five. Two star one is two plus two plus one, which is five too. It stays. Three choices are out, so choice number three is our answer.
at: is two plus one plus two
so choice number three is our answer

slides.say: [pause] Ruling out the other three already answers the question. Now let's see why choice number three works for every a and b. One example can't show that, so we swap the letters in the rule itself. b star a means b times a, plus b, plus a.

b times a is the same as a times b, and b plus a is the same as a plus b. So b star a is a b plus a plus b, which is exactly a star b, for every a and b. Choice number three. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next question.
